titulo: Private Lander Carrying NASA Experiments Lands on the Moon

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Texto recortado por párrafos; sin cambios en las frases.

parrafos: The lander, called Blue Ghost, was built by the American company Firefly Aerospace. The spacecraft touched down March 2 on the part of the moon’s near side called Mare Crisium. The near side of the moon is the side facing Earth.

Officials at Firefly’s Mission Control center near Austin, Texas, confirmed the successful landing. The chief engineer for the Blue Ghost mission, Will Coogan, announced to excited workers: “We’re on the moon.”

The officials said the spacecraft landed in the right position and was operating normally. The successful touchdown makes Firefly the first private company to land a spacecraft on the moon without crashing or having a major problem.

Blue Ghost is named after a rare kind of firefly found in the U.S. The four-legged lander is two meters tall and 3.5 meters wide. It launched in mid-January from Florida, carrying 10 experiments for the American space agency NASA.

In a statement, NASA said the 10 experiments are designed to operate on the surface of the moon for one lunar day, which is about 14 Earth days. The Associated Press reported that NASA paid $101 million for the spacecraft and $44 million for the equipment it carried.

It was the third mission under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program. The program aims to turn over the country’s major space missions to private companies to reduce costs. Several other companies are part of the program.

Another lander, called Athena, is set to attempt a moon landing on March 6. That four-meter-tall spacecraft was built and operated by Houston-based Intuitive Machines. It will land on another part of the moon, about 160 kilometers from the lunar south pole.

A third lander from private Japanese company ispace will attempt a moon landing in about three months. The lander, called Resilience, shared its rocket ride with Blue Ghost. But it took a longer path to the moon. The company is also attempting to land on the moon for the second time. Its first lander crashed in 2023.

NASA has said it aims to have two private landers launch to the moon each year, realizing some missions will fail. The space agency’s top science officer is Nicky Fox. She told the AP the latest launches “open up a whole new way for us to get more science to space and to the moon."

In the past, NASA’s successful moon landings involving astronauts cost billions of dollars. But Firefly chief Jason Kim said the private companies now building and launching spacecraft have a limited budget and the spacecraft operate robotically.
titulo_es: Un módulo de aterrizaje privado con experimentos de la NASA se posa en la Luna
resumen_es: Blue Ghost, de la empresa Firefly Aerospace, se convierte en la primera nave privada que aterriza en la Luna sin incidentes, dentro del programa de la NASA que encarga misiones a empresas para reducir costes.

ideas_clave.idea: Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost lander touched down on the near side of the moon on 2 March, to the delight of mission control in Texas.
It is the first private spacecraft to reach the lunar surface without crashing or suffering a serious problem.
The lander carries ten NASA experiments meant to run for one lunar day, and NASA paid about 145 million dollars in total.
The mission belongs to a NASA programme that hands major space missions over to private firms in order to cut costs.
Two other private landers, one American and one Japanese, are due to attempt landings in the coming months.
NASA plans two private launches a year, accepting some failures, because robotic missions with limited budgets are far cheaper than past crewed landings.

resumen_modelo: The text reports that Blue Ghost, a lander built by the American company Firefly Aerospace, touched down on 2 March in a region of the moon's near side known as Mare Crisium. Having landed upright and operating normally, it made Firefly the first private company to reach the moon without crashing or suffering a major failure. Launched from Florida in January, the spacecraft carries ten NASA experiments designed to work for one lunar day, roughly two Earth weeks; the agency paid 101 million dollars for the lander and 44 million for the equipment. This mission is the third within a NASA programme that entrusts major space missions to private firms in order to reduce costs. Other attempts are imminent: Athena, built by a Houston company, is to land near the lunar south pole, while the Japanese firm ispace will make a second attempt after crashing in 2023. NASA aims to send two private landers a year, accepting that some will fail, since these robotic missions with limited budgets are far cheaper than the crewed landings of the past, which cost billions.
